extracted.intended_audience: People and professionals needing accurate centimeters↔feet+inches conversions (general public, travelers, contractors, designers, healthcare, scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: A practical conversion guide and calculator showing exact factors, step-by-step methods, tables, precision/rounding advice, common mistakes, and implementation details for converting centimeters (and meters) to feet and inches for everyday, construction, medical, and scientific use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact conversion factor (1 inch = 2.54 cm)
rubrics_metrics.description: 1 inch = 2.54 centimeters exactly (established by the 1959 International Yard and Pound Agreement); derived factors include 1 cm = 0.393701 inches and 1 m = 3.28084 feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the authoritative basis for all conversions; the page cites the 1959 agreement and official sources (NIST, BIPM, ISO). Use the exact 2.54 cm per inch relationship rather than approximations to avoid systematic errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-step conversion method (cm → inches → feet + inches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide centimeters by 2.54 to get total inches; divide total inches by 12 to get decimal feet; take the whole number as feet; multiply the decimal portion by 12 to get remaining inches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step-by-step example given (175 cm → 68.898 in → 5 ft + 8.898 in ≈ 5′8.9″). Recommended for accuracy because it uses the exact inch definition; express final inches as decimal or convert to common fractions (¼, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32).

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct conversion method (meters → feet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiply meters by 3.28084 to get decimal feet, then take the whole number as feet and multiply remainder by 12 to get inches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provided as an alternative (Method 2) and noted as convenient for quick estimates, but the page warns direct meter→feet can introduce tiny rounding errors compared to the two-step inch-based method. Use only for rough estimates or when slight imprecision is acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rounding and precision guidance by application
rubrics_metrics.description: Different applications require different rounding levels: for heights, nearest quarter-inch is usually sufficient; for construction/carpentry, nearest sixteenth-inch or better; for scientific/engineering, keep at least 4–5 decimal places; everyday estimates can use nearest inch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide gives concrete recommendations (quarter-inch vs sixteenth-inch) and a 'pro tip' to round only the final inches value. It links precision needs to use cases like passport/medical vs construction/engineering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep extra decimal places until final rounding (avoid early rounding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not round intermediate results; keep extra decimal places during calculations and round only the final displayed inches value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained under 'Common Conversion Mistakes' (Mistake 3). Examples show how early rounding changes final feet+inches outcomes (e.g., rounding 68.898 vs 68.4). The page explicitly recommends preserving precision through intermediate steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct constants (avoid crude approximations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use exact constants (1 in = 2.54 cm; 1 m = 39.3701 in; 1 m = 3.28084 ft). Avoid using approximations like 2.5 or 25.4 or 3.28 when precision matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page warns common mistakes: confusing 2.54 with 25.4 (factor of 10 error), using 2.5 instead of 2.54 (~1.6% error), or 3.28 instead of 3.28084. For construction and precision work, these approximations are discouraged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate feet and inches by dividing by 12
rubrics_metrics.description: After getting total inches, divide by 12 to obtain feet and remainder inches; forgetting this step leaves you with total inches rather than feet+inches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as 'Mistake 2' — many people stop after getting total inches. The guide emphasizes this as an essential step in producing the conventional feet′in″ format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express decimal inches as usable fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert decimal inches into common practical fractions (1/4, 1/2, 3/4, 1/8, 1/16, 1/32) for display and use in construction/DIY contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The site provides tables and examples showing fractional equivalents (1/32 and 1/16 columns) and suggests rounding to the nearest practical fraction depending on the application. Examples show conversion to 7/8, 3/4, 1/16, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Input validation and flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Accepts whole centimeters or decimals (e.g., 175.5 cm); rejects invalid inputs (negative values, non-numeric characters); input range 0 to 9999 cm (0 to 99.99 meters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implementation notes: the converter supports decimal input and enforces sensible input bounds. The page documents validation behavior and acceptable input formats for reliable operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation precision and verification practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal calculations use 64-bit floating-point (15–17 significant digits); conversion claimed 'exact to floating-point precision limits'; reverse verification (convert result back to cm) should match input.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide explains methodology: cm × 0.393701 → total inches → feet + inches; it claims zero conversion error aside from floating-point limits and recommends reverse-checking results. Display rounding only affects presentation, not internal precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display precision and fractional-equivalent support
rubrics_metrics.description: Displays feet+inches with decimal inches and fractional equivalents (1/16, 1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1/32) and offers quick-reference charts for common heights and a printable table for 100–220 cm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The site offers downloadable Excel/Word/PDF versions, a full conversion table, and multiple fraction-resolution displays so users can choose the presentation best suited to their needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of international foot standard (not U.S. survey foot)
rubrics_metrics.description: The converter implements the international foot (1 ft = 0.3048 m exactly); the U.S. survey foot is deprecated and not used here.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Documented under 'Limitations and Scope'—clarifies which foot definition is applied to avoid ambiguity in specialized surveying contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency, authoritative sourcing, and traceability
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversion formulas, assumptions, and sources are disclosed and referenced (NIST SP 811, ISO 80000-3:2019, BIPM SI Brochure, 1959 Federal Register adoption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page emphasizes provenance of constants and verification against authoritative standards. It encourages confidence by citing standards and describing how conversions are computed and verified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common conversion mistakes to avoid (explicit list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enumerated common errors: confusing 2.54 with 25.4; forgetting to divide by 12; rounding too early; using crude conversion factors like 3.28 instead of 3.28084.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each listed mistake includes an explanation and illustrative consequence (e.g., 25.4 yields answers ten times too large). Users are advised how to avoid these pitfalls and when approximations are acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application-specific guidance and use-case examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Provides contextual examples and recommended practices for height measurements, construction/architecture, furniture/interior design, medical/scientific applications, e-commerce/product specs, visas/immigration, and sports profiles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide ties precision and presentation choices to concrete use cases (e.g., quarter-inch rounding for height; sixteenth-inch for carpentry) and gives worked examples (175 cm, 190 cm, 200 cm, etc.) to illustrate outcomes in real-world contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privacy and client-side processing assurance
rubrics_metrics.description: Conversion math runs entirely in the browser; values entered are not sent to the server; methodology is public and verifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is documented as a privacy guarantee and as part of trustworthiness: users can verify calculations locally and the tool claims no server-side logging of inputs.
